Lignocellulosic biomass (LCB) is an ample and alternative renewable energy resource that can be effectively converted to obtain biofuels, biochemicals, and other value-added materials (Modak et al., 2021a). LCB, present primarily in the plant cell walls, can A.R. Mankar et al. Bioresource Technology 345 (2022) 126528 also be used as a potential substitute to the conventional fossil reserves and hence play a critical role in meeting future energy needs. LCB is a highly complex architecture wherein the cellulosic and hemi-cellulosic fractions are sandwiched between the lignin layers, overall resulting into the formation of covalently bonded strong lignin-carbohydrate complex (Mankar et al., 2021a). To achieve the maximum output of the LCB, it is essential to separate, extract, and transform chemically these biopolymers i.e., cellulose, hemicellulose, and lignin into valuable products. Compared to other constituents in biomass, the water-insoluble aromatic polymer – lignin, is an attractive feedstock for obtaining value-added products owing to its high carbon, low oxygen content, biodegradability, and high thermal stability, among many others. However, structural complexity inherent to lignin and variability in its concentration in different LCB are major hindrance in lignin depolymerization in high quantity and high purity. Further, chemical modifications in lignin structure during pretreatment also affects its effective utilization in analysing and obtaining valuable lignols. While the current pretreatment methods have focussed largely on the extraction of cellulose and hemicellulose, separation of lignin from LCB still remains a big challenge and is therefore the key to LCB valorisation. Conventional pretreatment approaches such as organosolv, alkaline, acid, and enzymatic methods show either lower efficiency in overcoming the strong interactive energies of lignin-carbohydrate complex or lignin contamination with solvents, ultimately exhibiting lower lignin extraction potential. Ionic liquids (ILs), in this regard, have attracted significant attention due to their ability to partially or completely dissolve lignin with high extraction efficacy. However, serious concerns related to the greenness and toxicity of ILs in addition to its high viscosity and high cost render the use of ILs for LCB pretreatment (Pandey et al., 2021). Moreover, long-term recyclability and extensive postprocessing methods during ILs pretreatment also inhibit their practical applications in industrial scale-up (Mankar et al., 2021b). Recently, the development of deep eutectic solvents (DESs) has opened up new avenues in the area of lignin extraction and its subse- quent valorisation (Huang et al., 2021; Liang et al., 2021; Mankar et al., 2021c). DESs are low melting solutions obtained as a result of mixing hydrogen bond donors (HBDs) with hydrogen bond acceptors (HBAs). These neoteric eutectic mixtures resemble ILs in possessing similar physicochemical properties and are therefore also called as analogues of ILs (Chourasia et al., 2021; Pandey et al., 2021). Moreover, DESs offer significant advantages over ILs in easy of synthesis with high atom ef- ficiency, no purification steps, insensitivity to water, non-toxicity, environmentally benign nature, and technoeconomic feasibility in their use for extraction, analytics, electrochemistry, biotechnology, catalysis, and synthesis amongst various other industrial applications. Owing to the multitude of advantages DESs exhibit over ILs, suitability of these green solvents as alternatives to ILs in pretreatment of LCB have been extensively studied. Promising results in use of DESs for lignin dissolution and extraction have been reported in earlier studies (Alvarez-Vasco et al., 2016; Liang et al., 2021; Ong et al., 2021; Tan et al., 2019; Wang et al., 2021; Xu et al., 2016). In a recent study by Huang et al. (Huang et al., 2021), ChCl/guaiacol-based DES with AlCl3 was employed for the pretreatment of wheat straw at 130 °C for 1 h giving a lignin removal of 43.3%. Similarly, Wang et al. (Wang et al., 2020) reported 69.9% of delignification of poplar at 160 °C for 3 h using lignin-based phenolic compound p-hydroxybenzoic acid as HBD and ChCl as HBA. Ong et al. (Ong et al., 2021) investigated the pretreatment (120 °C, 4 h) of oil palm fronds (OPF) with NaOH-DES (ChCl/urea) combined with ultrasound (60% amplitude, 30 min duration). The results showed a significantly higher lignin removal of 47% for combined pretreatment compared to 30.9% for pretreatment without ultrasound, thus indicating a synergistic effect to be responsible for improving the pretreatment efficiency. In another study, Wang et al. (Wang et al., 2021) reported the hydrothermal-DES (ChCl/lactic acid) pretreatment of moso bamboo. Under optimum conditions (140 °C, 6 h), a delignification of 80.1 wt% was achieved. Thus, the severe conditions are required for the pretreatment of biomass with longer durations (1 to 6 h) to get effective delignification. Therefore, microwave heating has proved to be an efficient pretreatment method for biomass delignifica- tion due to its fast and uniform heating at molecular level, which helps in significantly reducing the reaction time from hours to minutes (Mankar et al., 2021c). A study by Liu et al. (Liu et al., 2017) compared the conventional and microwave heating for the pretreatment of poplar using ChCl: oxalic acid DES. The results showed that it took only 3 min to get a lignin removal of 80% under microwave heating compared to 9 h required to get a similar yield under conventional heating. The use of microwave heating in combination with DES appeals to be a promising technology for the delignification of biomass from different sources which is still in its infancy. Therefore, in-depth and rigorous research is further required to explore their applicability in treating biomass to isolate lignin. In this regard, the current study aims to use ChCl-carboxylic acid based eutectic mixtures in the treatment of coconut coir, a fibrous external portion of the fruit of Cocus nucifera (coconut). In India, coconut is celebrated as a symbol of prosperity, a blessing of nature, a propitious object of ceremony, a useful item of handicraft, and an essential cooking ingredient. However, coconut coir having high lignin content (~30-40 %), largely remains unused in most of these cases and hence is a source of large amounts of waste. In this study, a systematic investigation of the microwave-mediated use of different DESs in the extraction of lignin from this waste – coconut coir, in high yield and purity was done to improve the overall energy efficiency of the process and efficiency. Further studies were performed to understand the effect of pretreatment time, temperature, and HBA: HBD molar ratio on lignin extractability. DES extracted lignin was further characterized by attenuated total reflectance fourier transform infrared spectroscopy (ATR-FTIR), thermogravimetric analysis (TGA), derivative of weight loss (DTG) as a function of temperature, nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR), gel permeation chromatography (GPC) techniques. Further, the valorization of the extracted lignin to valuable aromatics was done via catalytic transfer hydrogenation (CTH) and the process parameters like temperature, time, and catalyst dosage were optimized to maximize the bio-oil yield. Overall, the objective of the present study is to develop a green, cost-effective, mild, and efficient process for the extraction of lignin in high purity from coconut coir and its further valorization into valuable chemicals. 2. When the lignin extraction was done using ChCl: urea, negligible lignin extraction (<1%) was achieved, indicating that the absence of acidity in urea might be responsible for the low lignin yield. However, a significant extraction of lignin from the coconut coir was observed when the pretreatment were performed using ChCl: carboxylic acid based DESs. The hydrogen-bond acidity (α) of the DES is previously reported to govern the cleavage of lignin-carbohydrate-complex (LCC) in the biomass (Liang et al., 2021). ChCl: OA DES gave the highest lignin extraction of 37.8% as it had the highest α value of 1.32. Further, when ChCl: LA DES was used for the pretreatment of coconut coir, a lignin extraction of 35.3% was observed. A slight decrease in the lignin extraction compared to ChCl: OA DES can be related to the lower α value (1.17). Similar trend of results was ob- tained for ChCl: AA and ChCl: BA DES based on the α values (Fig. 1a). The effect of aliphatic chain length of the HBD on the lignin extraction ability was also studied by comparing the ChCl: AA and ChCl: BA DES. When ChCl: AA DES was used for the pre-treatment of coconut coir, a lignin yield of 15.2% was achieved. However, when the ChCl: BA DES was applied for the pre-treatment, the lignin yield decreased to half (7.6%). The results indicated that increase in alkyl chain length of the HBD reduced the ability of that particular DES to extract lignin. The electron density of the oxygen in the hydroxyl group of carboxylic acid increases with the increase in chain length of the electron donating alkyl group. As a result, the strength of the hydrogen bond between the ox- ygen and hydrogen increases thus limiting the ability to donate proton. Therefore, the DES with shorter chain length showed better activity for lignin removal as it improved the solvent-solute interaction by easily donating the proton (Teles et al., 2017). It is also noteworthy to mention here that the pKa value of the HBDs in the DES also plays an important role in indicating the lignin extraction ability of a particular DES. The results of lignin extraction from coconut coir are in agreement with the pKa values, e.g., ChCl: AA (pKa = 4.76) showed better lignin yield compared to ChCl: BA (pKa = 4.82). In case of ChCl: LA DES, higher lignin extraction yield of 35.3% was achieved because of the lower pKa value (3.86). However, despite slightly higher lignin yield of 37.8% in case of ChCl: OA DES owing to the higher acidity (pKa1 = 1.46, pKa2 = 4.4), a significant charring of the coconut coir recovered after the pre-treatment, was observed. High acidity of ChCl: OA can be attributed for the charring of the coconut coir. Moreover, release of CO2 is also reported due to the activation of carboxyl groups in the OA. However, it is desired to recover the lignin free coconut coir after the pretreatment so that it can be further utilized to produce fermentable sugars via enzymatic hydrolysis which can further be con- verted to bioethanol. Therefore, ChCl: LA DES was used for further re- actions as the solid (coconut coir) was recovered compared to the charred solid obtained in case of ChCl: OA DES. 3.1.2. Effect of molar ratio of ChCl to LA on lignin extraction To understand the role of ChCl and LA in the extraction of lignin, experiments were performed in the presence of ChCl: LA DES with different molar ratios (1:2, 1:4, 1:6, 1:8). When the experiment was performed in the presence of pure LA at 150 °C for 20 min, a low lignin yield of 16.9% was observed. However, when the extraction run was performed in the presence of ChCl: LA (1:2), a significant increase in the lignin yield from 16.9% (in the absence of ChCl) to 73.9% was achieved. The results indicated that ChCl played a synergistic effect with LA in the extraction of lignin from the coconut coir, thus resulting in higher lignin yield. The delignification of coconut coir was initiated via the cleavage of LCC. This involved weakening of strong hydrogen bonding present within coconut coir due to the formation of hydrogen bonds between the hydroxyl group of lignin/carbohydrate and chloride ions of ChCl: LA DES (Liu et al., 2017). Additionally, the role of LA in the extraction of lignin was also accessed. As such, the molar ratio of LA in ChCl: LA DES was increased from 1:2 to 1:4. A two-fold increase in LA concentration in the DES resulted in enhanced lignin yield, i.e., the lignin yield was found to be 73.9% and 82% for 1:2 and 1:4 ratio of ChCl: LA, respectively. The results indicated that the increase in LA content in DES has promoted the extraction ability of DES, thus improving the overall yield of the extracted lignin. The reason for the improved delignification efficiency was the promoted cleavage of LCC due to the increased hydrogen-bond acidity associated with the LA content (Chen et al., 2019). However, when the reactions were performed at higher ChCl: LA molar ratios (>1:4), the lignin yield was found to decrease as shown in Fig. 1d. Overall, the results indicated that both LA and ChCl plays an equally important role in the extraction of lignin and an optimum molar ratio is required to get the maximum extraction efficiency. In the present study, a ChCl: LA with a molar ratio of 1:4 was found to be the optimum DES as it gave the highest yield of extracted lignin (82%). 3.1.4. Comparison of conventional and microwave heating and DES recyclability The effect of mode of heating on the efficiency of lignin extraction from coconut coir was also compared. Experiment was conducted in an oil-bath with 0.5 g coconut coir and 15 g ChCl: LA (1:4) DES for lignin extraction under conventional heating. When the reaction was per- formed at 150 °C for 20 min, only 13.5% lignin was extracted. Under similar reaction conditions, when the reaction was performed under microwave heating, the lignin extraction was 6 times higher (82%) compared to conventional heating. To further improve the lignin extraction under conventional heating, the reaction time was extended to 8 h which resulted in only 46% of lignin extraction. Besides, the H factor for the conventional heating (150 °C, 8 h) was also significantly higher (1334.1) compared to the significantly lower H factor (55.5) for microwave heating (150 °C, 20 min), while the lignin extraction was also approximately half of that for microwave heating. Lower lignin extraction ability using DES under severe reaction conditions in case of conventional heating is a result of heating via conduction which involves heat losses due to temperature gradients. On the contrary, an electro- magnetic field is applied in case of microwave heating which facilitates vibration and rotation of the polar molecules present in LCB, hence releasing heat at faster rate (Mankar et al., 2021c). This prevents any heat losses during microwave heating and ensures uniform heating. Moreover, the microwave radiation helps in increasing the molecular polarity and also maximizes the ionic characteristics of DES, resulting in better lignin extraction at lower reaction time (Liu et al., 2017). It is reported for microwave heating that the polar groups present in the complex LCB structure can further create hot spots and led to an explosion effect within the particles. As a result, the disruption of LCB complex takes places resulting in enhanced lignin extraction. Overall, the microwave heating was highly effective in extracting lignin from coconut coir in high yields using ChCl: LA DES compared to the conventional heating under milder reaction conditions. The recyclability of DES is an important parameter in terms of development of a sustainable future biorefinery. In this study, we have recycled the DES and reused it for the extraction of lignin from coconut coir to check its recyclability. All the recycle runs were performed under the optimized reaction conditions (150 °C, 20 min, ChCl: LA (1:4) DES). The DES showed considerable lignin extraction in the recycle runs. When the DES was recycled after the first run, the lignin yield was found to be slightly reduced from 82% (fresh run) to 78.1%. Additionally, a lignin yield of 75.5% and 71.8% was achieved for second and third recycle run, respectively. However, a further gradual decrease in the lignin yield to 68.5 % was seen after the fourth cycle. The probable reason for the reduction in the extraction ability might be the loss of some amount of DES during the workup procedures which might have reduced the overall acidity of the DES reaction system. In earlier reported literatures, Wu et al. (Wu et al., 2014) studied the organosolv pretreatment of hybrid poplar without catalyst using 80% aqueous solution of methanol at 220 °C for 30 min and a lignin yield of 45.5% was reported. Further, to improve the lignin yield under milder reaction conditions, some studies have reported the use of acid/alkali catalysts. Zhong et al. (Zhong et al., 2021) investigated effect of alkali catalyst (NaOH) on the organosolv pretreatment (methanol/water (65/ 35 v/v)). A lignin yield of 64.3% was reported at 80 °C, 1 h using 2 wt.% NaOH dosage. In another study, Mondylaksita et al. (Mondylaksita et al., 2020) reported the acid-catalyzed (0.07% H2SO4) organosolv pretreat- ment (ethanol) of Oil palm empty fruit bunch. Under the pretreatment conditions of 210 °C and 1.5 h, a lignin yield of 64.9% was reported. In a similar study by Chen et al. (Chen et al., 2021), a ternary solvent system (acetone/phenoxyethanol/water) was utilized for the pretreatment of Amorpha using H2SO4 as catalyst. Under optimum conditions (130 °C, 70 min, 0.15 M H2SO4) a lignin yield of 35.6% was reported. Wei et al. (Wei et al., 2021) compared the acid and alkali catalyzed pretreatment of bagasse using organosolv approach (ethylene glycol/water (9/1 v/ v)). When the pretreatment was done at 130 °C for 1 h, a lignin yield of 39.2% and 47.9% were reported for ethylene glycol/H2O-HCl and ethylene glycol/H2O-NaOH, respectively. The major drawback of organosolv process is volatility, flammability, high cost, and solvent recovery. Moreover, recyclability of the homogenous acid and alkali catalyst is also a major challenge. In addition, the acid pretreatment involves the problems like corrosion and formation of fermentation in- hibitors while the alkali pretreatment is mainly associated with high costs for neutralization of slurry (Mankar et al., 2021c). Thus, our study is advantageous over these reported established methods in terms on cost-effectiveness, biodegradability, ease of synthesis, and recyclability of the DESs. ## 3.2. TGA Thermal stability of the lignin was studied using TGA analysis (see e-supplementary material). The initial weight loss between 25 and 155 °C corresponded to the removal of moisture and volatiles with low molecular weight (Rashid et al., 2016). The moisture content of Kraft lignin was significantly higher (7.9 wt.%) compared to the extracted lignin (4.1 wt.%) as can be seen from the TGA curves. Second major weight loss occurred between 156 and 550 °C which is associated with the fragmentation of several inter-unit linkages (C—O—C, C—C) giving products like phenolics, gases, etc (Rashid et al., 2016). Moreover, it is reported that the cracking of methoxy groups in the lignin leads to the release of methane gas while CO gas is released due to C=O, C—O—C cleavage in a temperature range of 400 to 700 °C. Further, at higher temperatures (551 to 800 °C), aromatic rings undergo thermal decomposition producing char or coke (Rashid et al., 2016). From the TGA plots, it can be clearly seen that the lignin is not completely degraded even at 800 °C due to the presence of high-condensed residual char (Schorr et al., 2014). The Kraft lignin showed a residual char of 47.8% while the DES extracted lignin had a residual charge of 33.4%, indicating the presence of more condensed C—C linkages in case of Kraft lignin compared to the extracted lignin (Schorr et al., 2014). The lower number of C—C linkages in the extracted lignin might help in its easier valorization to aromatics. ### 3.2.3. The maximum weight loss rate (wt.%/°C) of 0.08 was seen for Kraft lignin which was four times compared to the extracted lignin (0.02), thus indicating more moisture content in the Kraft lignin. Further, a sharp maxima was recorded at 315 °C which showed a maximum weight loss of 0.2 for Kraft lignin and 0.14 for extracted lignin due to the cleavage of β-O-4 linkage (Kim et al., 2013). The peaks between 0.8 and 2 ppm corresponded to the aliphatic hydrocarbon region mainly consisting of primary, secondary, and tertiary alkyl groups (Deepa and Dhepe, 2015; Li et al., 2020; Rashid et al., 2016). The peaks between 1.4 and 2.2 ppm corresponds to the proton of aliphatic acetates while the signals at 2.2 to 2.5 ppm represents the proton of aromatic acetates (Rashid et al., 2016). Optimization of reaction parameters for catalytic transfer hydrogenation (CTH) The lignin extracted from the coconut coir using ChCl: LA DES was further valorised by employing Ru/C catalyst for CTH in the presence of isopropyl alcohol. Therefore, reactions were performed in a temperature range of 80 to 180 °C for 20 min in a microwave reactor to study the effect of temperature on the bio-oil yield. When the reaction was done at 80 °C, a bio-oil yield of 28.5% was achieved. Further, when the reactions were carried out at elevated temperatures of 100 °C and 120 °C, the yield of bio-oil increased to 32.7% and 38.8%, respectively. The results suggested that the depolymerization of lignin is temperature dependent, i.e., increases with increase in temperature and vice-versa. However, when the reaction temperature was further increased (>120 °C), a reduction in the bio-oil yield was observed (Table 4), with a lowest bio-oil yield of 25.8% at 180 °C. The reason for the decrease in the bio-oil yield is the decomposition or condensation of the lignin derived products, which might lead to char formation at higher temperatures (Hita et al., 2018; Long et al., 2015). Therefore, 120 °C was considered as the optimum reaction temperature as highest bio-oil yield was achieved at this temperature. The reaction time is another crucial parameter which governs the bio-oil yield in the CTH reactions. Therefore, a series of reactions were performed at 120 °C and the reaction time was varied between 10 and 60 min. When the reaction was conducted for 10 min, a bio-oil yield of 29.9% was achieved. Moreover, further increasing the reaction time to 20 min led to improved bio-oil yield of 38.8%. But, when the reaction time was >20 min, a decline in the bio-oil yield was observed (Table 4) and only 26.1% yield was achieved at 60 min. The probable reason for the decreasing trend in the bio-oil yield at longer reaction time might be the re-polymerization/re-condensation of the reactive intermediates which may lead to humin/char formation as confirmed from the increased solid residue (Long et al., 2015). Therefore, further reactions were performed for a reaction time of 20 min as maximum bio-oil yield was achieved at this time. Another important parameter which affects the yield of bio-oil in the CTH of lignin is the catalyst dosage. The catalyst plays an important role in cleavage of the linkages in the lignin to produce desired valuable aromatic compounds. When the reactions were performed at 120 °C for 20 min at 1.5 mg Ru/C catalyst, a bio-oil yield of 25.3% was observed. Under optimum conditions, the GC-MS results (see e-supplementary material) showed a highly selective formation of two major products namely, 1,2-Benzenedicarboxylic acid, dibutyl ester (48%) and 1,2-Benzenedicarboxylic acid, dioctyl ester (47.5%), which are commonly used as plasticizers. These compounds are formed via cleavage of the linkages present in the DES extracted lignin via hydrogenation/hydrogenolysis reactions. In addition, minor products like 1,2-Benzenedicarboxylic acid, butyl diethylhexyl ester (1.7%) and hexanedioic acid, bis (2-ethylhexyl) ester (2.8%) were also detected. Conclusions A practical approach towards effective pretreatment of coconut coir using DESs to extract high purity lignin is demonstrated in this study. Under optimum conditions (150 °C, 20 min, ChCl: LA DES), a lignin yield of 82% was achieved using microwave heating. The ability of DES to extract lignin was directly correlated with their Kamlet Taft parameters and pKa values. The extracted lignin had all the functional groups corresponding to the native lignin and a purity of >95%. Further, the CTH of extracted lignin gave a bio-oil yield of 38.8% under mild reaction conditions (120 °C, 20 min) using Ru/C catalyst.
